sentences.text: The skull of this creature measures exactly 71.2 cm in length.
Its eight caniniform teeth tilt forward and remain smooth except for striations near the jaw attachment.
The cervical ribs possess a single head, a feature shared with other Cretaceous pliosaurs.
The species is defined by a moderately long symphysis bearing eight pairs of nearly circular, smooth teeth.
The holotype appears to be the only known fossil of the entire genus.
Scientists have recorded just one fossil occurrence of this animal.
The origin of the holotype specimen CM 2815 remains uncertain, with conflicting reports placing it in either the Belle Fourche Shale or the Hailey Shales Formation.
This animal lived entirely in water and moved using paddle-like flippers via paraxial propulsion, much like sea turtles.
Although initially described as a pliosauroid due to its short neck, it actually belongs to the order Plesiosauria.
Later research classifies it as a member of the family Polycotylidae within the clade Occultonectia.
In 2018, Fischer and colleagues named the clade Occultonectia to include Plesiopleurodon, the Richmond pliosaur, and Sulcusuchus erraini.
Plesiopleurodon lived during the Cenomanian stage, approximately 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
Carpenter noted that Plesiopleurodon wellesi most closely resembles the European Oxfordian species Liopleurodon ferox.
It is debated whether the short neck of Plesiopleurodon definitively places it in the pliosauroid group, as later research shows neck length varies within both plesiosauroids and pliosauroids.
